utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries were announced, therefore the witness can be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Guzina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we start, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jeremy. You'll find him to your right. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Jeremy, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Guzina.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: At various points today I'll be referring you to parts of your statement, D514.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Therefore, I would ask the court officer to provide a clean copy of that statement to you, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, your nickname is Sesa, correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sesa or Seso.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And that's S-e-s-a, correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sound is s-h, sh.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Between paragraphs 6 and 32 of your witness statement, D514, it appears you're discussing events that transpired between February and June 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Between paragraph 6 and 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, I'll start with a few questions relating to those paragraphs in your statement. Turning firstly to paragraph 20 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And that's e-court page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: -- you mention that an Enver Hodzic and his son came to the Serbian barricade by a swimming pool. Now, is it correct that this swimming pool is located to the south of Ilidza near a park and an athletics field?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a football field, the rest is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P3, and I'd like to go to e-court page 78 of that document. It's the Sarajevo map book.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Guzina, as this is coming up, it's a map that depicts the areas of Ilidza, Sokolovic Kolonija, Butmir, and most of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I'm looking for e-court page 78. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, directing your attention to the main road that runs south from Ilidza towards Sokolovic Kolonija, is it correct that the Serbian barricade you referred to in paragraph 20 of your statement is next to the swimming pool that we see located on this route? Just left of the centre of the picture as we see it.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Taking the pen that you used yesterday, which the usher will assist you with, could you please draw a circle around the location of the Serbian barricade on this map.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's about here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I tender that image as marked by the witness as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document as marked by the witness receives number P6587, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, in paragraph 11 of your statement, e-court page 3 in the English and 4 in the B/C/S, you mention the Ilidza Municipal Assembly chairperson Radomir Kezunovic, and a conversation that you had with him sometime in March 1992. Now, it's correct, isn't, that Mr. Kezunovic was the president of the Assembly of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza at this time?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And it's also correct, isn't it, that the Serbs from Ilidza began organising political structures of their own prior to January 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They started organising themselves at Ilidza as soon as the elections were over.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And what was the date that the elections were over?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not a politician. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 03638.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, sir, while this is being brought up, I'll tell you it's a decision dated 3 January 1992 from Mr. Kezunovic, and it proclaims the establishment of the Serb municipality Municipal Assembly of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, we see this is signed by Mr. Kezunovic. And can you confirm at this time, on the 3rd of January, 1992, he was the president of the Assembly of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't see why you are questioning me about this. At this time I was not in the SDS nor was I part of any authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not for you to question the reasons why these questions are put to you. Answer them. If you do know, please tell us. If you don't know, tell us as well. But it's the Prosecutor, under the supervision of the Bench, which considers what questions are there to be put. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, I will repeat --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In the preamble to this decision there is a reference to the will of the Serbian people from the area of the Ilidza municipality expressed at a plebiscite on the 9th and 10th of November, 1991. Mr. Guzina, you would agree that this shows that, in fact, the Serbs from Ilidza were taking steps to organise political structures of their own prior to January 1992, yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that the Serbs from the SDS ticket implemented that, but I was a caterer. I had my own restaurant. These things didn't interest me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender that document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 3638 receives number P6588, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, it's also correct, isn't it, that the Serbs in Ilidza began arming citizens of Serbian nationality during 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Could you explain this to me in more detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's take a look at a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please see Exhibit P3792.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, coming up on the screen before you is a report by the public security station of Ilidza. It's dated the 20th of September, 1993, but it relates to -- in part to events in Ilidza during 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see in the third paragraph down a reference to: "At the beginning of 1991, during illegal meetings organised by Kovac Tomislav, Commander of the Ilidza Public Security Station at the time, policemen of Serbian nationality were informed that the war option for realisation of national interests was being increasingly promoted. Aside from the obligation that Serbs gather up and prepare for war through those meetings that took place in Dobrinja --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're reading, Mr. Jeremy. Speed of speech goes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'll slow down, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "... Ilidza and Blazuj, it was also agreed that intense activity should be undertaken to arm citizens of Serbian nationality." Firstly, Mr. Guzina, you mention Tomislav Kovac in paragraph 11 of your statement. You were familiar with this person, correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander of the police station at Ilidza, or chief, whatever it's called.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you would agree that this document shows that actions were being taken to arm citizens of Serbian nationality during 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time all sorts of stories circulated. I'm telling you what I know. At that time, I was not part of these structures and I didn't know about many things because I was running a restaurant that was patronised by Serbs and Muslims and Croats alike, and people were good friends, staying up until all hours. I can only tell you about the time when the first roadblock or barricade went up in my area, my neighbourhood, Sokolovic Kolonija.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'm finished with that document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one question to the witness. Mr. Guzina, did you receive a weapon at this time-period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the barricade that I described, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What kind of weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] M-56. From Captain Jaslar, the man I described as representing this League for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Have you any recollection when, I mean a specific day or week or month, this hand-over took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I can't remember the date. But certainly in that period. After the barricade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because before that I wasn't even interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one or more questions for the witness as well, Mr. Jeremy. You said you were not interested in arming or being armed before the barricades appeared. Could you tell us when did you observe or hear about Muslims arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Long before the Serbs. I was running a restaurant and in a restaurant you get a lot of information, you hear people talking, you hear about many things, so I heard from the patrons that were Muslims were organising themselves. And after the Muslims did, they started organising themselves too. I heard about these things but I was not a part of them. Still, I cannot tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exact date, approximately, month? Month, year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1990, 1991, that's when the whole story began. As for the month, I really can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said it was before the Serbs started arming themselves. A minute ago you told us that as a restaurant owner, you had no idea about arming, et cetera. That you even provoked, to some extent, Mr. Jeremy saying, "Give me the details, and then I'll discuss it further with you." Now, in your statement, paragraph 26, you give all kind of details about who was arming, when, and the League of Yugoslavs, at the time you thought this was all the best option. Not a word about the SDS. How is it that you know the details about others arming, although you mentioned that the Serbs armed themselves as well, but there is not a word about who did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at that time people talked. I was nonstop in the restaurant, and Muslims, my friends, told me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say "at that time," I would like to know more about what time you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was more than 20 years ago. I'm talking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In 1991, what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that the Muslims were organising themselves, arming themselves, and Alija Izetbegovic, the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, visited a neighbour of mine three houses down, Enver Hodzic. There was a lot of talk in the restaurant between the Serbs and Muslims. We exchanged information, we who didn't want war. It's difficult to understand now after so much time and after the war, but that's how it was, and nobody expected a war of such intensity at that time. We just continued being friends, talking what to do, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs. It's difficult to put it in words now. I'm telling the truth, I'm telling things as they really were on the ground at that time. And people, after a few drinks in a restaurant, talk even more. I didn't see it with my own eyes but I heard it. That's how I put together this chronology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question to you was what exactly you heard. I haven't -- you have explained to us that there was a lot of talk and that you're telling us the truth, et cetera, but what you heard is apparently rather vague. Now let me follow-up. You said it was in 1991 that you heard these things. Did you hear about Serbs arming themselves or being armed also at that -- well, let's say, in the beginning of 1991? Or did that come later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few months later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The document that was just put to you which describes what happened in this respect states that it was in the beginning of 1991. I just put that to you so that you can comment on it if you wish to. I have one other question which is totally different area. The son of Enver Hodzic who came with his father, what was his age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before this answer, let me just say that Sokolovic Kolonija is not on this list of armament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was talking about the line stating: "At the beginning of 1991, during illegal meetings organised by Kovac Tomislav ... policemen of the Serb nationality were informed that the war option for realisation of national interests was being increasingly promoted." And then it continues how citizens were to be armed. That is what I refer to, and whether you are, let me see -- and do I understand that your village is not within the Ilidza municipality? Or is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim with full responsibility that I did not attend a single one of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one said you were. This report is about arming also in Ilidza. You told us that your village was not mentioned here. My question was whether your village is in Ilidza, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, it's not a village. It is a neighbourhood that was in the municipality of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so if Ilidza is mentioned as an area where weapons should be distributed, then your neighbourhood is not excluded from that although not specifically mentioned. That's apparently where we are. Then we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then my other question remains still unanswered. That is: What is the age of the son of Enver Hodzic you refer to who came with his father to Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly. Say, 15 or 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you wanted him to bring his son in order to guarantee your safety and you ask him to bring a 15- or 16-year-old son. Is that well understood from your statement in paragraph 20?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Jeremy. Can I just see the front page of this document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, were you a part of the Ilidza Territorial Defence by March 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After leaving Sokolovic Kolonija, I became a member of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And what was the date that you left Sokolovic Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly. I think it was the beginning of April. Now, was it the 4th or the 5th, I don't know. I cannot give you an answer as accurate as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So that's April 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please see Exhibit P3030.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, while this is being brought up, I can tell you it's a 2nd Military District document dated March 1992. And it's a report based on the assessment of the situation in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 11 in the English and 16 in the B/C/S of this document. Could we focus in on number 6, Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, this is a list that details enlisted Serb volunteers by municipality. Item 6 indicates that there were 2.800 individuals listed as Serb volunteers in Ilidza. At this time, you were one of those 2.800 volunteers; correct? Or you became one shortly after at the start of the April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, would it not be accurate to say that the document dates from the 20th of March. That's at least what I find on the first of 12 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what type of volunteers you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you a volunteer at that time of whatever kind in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember before the war that there was this proclamation of the Army of Yugoslavia that all reserve soldiers should come to the barracks in Lukavica. Now, whether this relates to that or -- I don't know what volunteers are the ones mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you never actively acted in any way, either by reporting yourself, in whatever way, as a volunteer on or before the 20th of March, 1992, in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain so that it would be clear to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would first please answer my question, then you can explain. And I add to my question: Act as a volunteer such that the military district could consider you to be among whatever kind of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not a volunteer. Not a volunteer of any kind. It was only after the check-point in Sokolovic Kolonija that I started asking around, asking people in the SDS, Zara Hrnjez [phoen] specifically, who was the representative of the SDS in Sokolovic Kolonija, asking how to go on. Until that period of time, I did not take part in anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, in paragraph 19 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I'm finished with this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, paragraph 19 of your statement you refer to a delegation that was made up yourself, Prstojevic, and Lukic. Here you're referring to a Nedjeljko Prstojevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not Zeljko. An elderly gentleman wasn't Zeljko, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment I cannot remember. He was my neighbour in Sokolovic Kolonija, but he's deceased. Believe me I cannot remember. It is Prstojevic, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, it's correct, isn't it, that in April 1992, there was a general mobilisation of all military-aged conscripts in the territory of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we call that general mobilisation? There was this organisation, all Serbs were called to report at the Territorial Defence to be deployed in certain locations in terms of the defence of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please see 65 ter 22938.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, this is a 6th April 1992 order on the implementation of general mobilisation from a Nedjeljko Prstojevic of the Ilidza Crisis Staff. Under item 1, this order calls for the general mobilisation of all military conscripts in the territory of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza between the ages of 18 to 60. Mr. Guzina, is this the general mobilisation that you just referred to in your previous answer?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would probably be it. That's what's written here, the 6th of April. And I think I said that it was around the 5th that we left Sokolovic Kolonija. It's possible that this is it. Yes, yes, it is. That's for sure. It's been signed, there is a stamp. Nedjeljko Prstojevic was president of the Crisis Staff in the municipality of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So you would confirm that the first name is Nedjeljko instead of Zeljko, where you said earlier that this is not his first name. But it's the same person, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mistake. This is Nedjeljko Prstojevic. He was president of the Crisis Staff, afterwards the president of the municipality of Ilidza, whereas the other one is a different Prstojevic who lived in Sokolovic Kolonija. Now, whether they are related, that is probably the case, but it's not one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Guzina, you responded to this general mobilisation order; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. By then I was already involved. Perhaps even a few days before this. Before leaving Sokolovic Kolonija, I was appointed commander of Sokolovic Kolonija on behalf of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender that document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22938 receives number P6589, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, it's correct, isn't it, that the Serbs were the ones who decided to move Croats and Muslims out of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please see Exhibit P470.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Guzina, while this is coming up, I'll tell you it's a 19 May 1992 decision from Nedjeljko Prstojevic who you just confirmed you knew to be the president of the Ilidza Crisis Staff. This decision states: "The moving out of Croats and Muslims from all territories of Ilidza Serb Municipality is allowed, apart from Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija and Hrasnica (prohibited from leaving)." Mr. Guzina, this document written by Nedjeljko Prstojevic shows that contrary to what you've just told us, that, in fact, it was the Serbs who decided to move Croats and Muslims out of Ilidza. Yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this document because I was not a member of the Crisis Staff, and this was written on the 19th of May, 1992, as far as I know, after the first attack against the municipality of Ilidza and our positions, after the killing of many Serbs. I know and I claim with full responsibility that the Muslims in the municipality of Ilidza voluntarily left their apartments and their houses, and they left wherever it was that they wanted to go, either towards Kiseljak or Sarajevo, nobody prevented them from doing so. But it is also a fact that nobody was driving them out. Now, what is mentioned here, Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Hrasnica, whether that has anything to do with this first attack, believe me, I don't know. But this is the first time I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, are you aware that Nedjeljko Prstojevic spoke at Republika Srpska Assemblies about efforts to remove non-Serbs from Serb-claimed territories in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. I wasn't following that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document, P4581. And as it is being brought up, I'll tell you it's from the Republika Srpska People's Assembly session 24 to 26 of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to -- one moment, I'll just get the -- could we go to the next page in this document. Your Honours, one moment, I'll just get the exact page reference. Court's indulgence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 66. And if we zoom in on the bottom half of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, here we see Mr. Prstojevic's address to this Assembly. He states: "... I have decided to say a few words and ask --"

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. I cannot see this. On my screen I cannot see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, the usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, either slowly read it to him or perhaps the best would be to enlarge and have only the B/C/S on the screen and that at the same time you read it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, could we enlarge the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not very clear, Witness, but we'll have to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, I'll quote you a few lines from that excerpt as follows: "... I have decided to say a few words and to ask a few questions that I am being asked by the citizens of Sarajevo; namely, when the Serbs started the uprising in Sarajevo and when they seized control over certain territories. There was no government or at least it was not known where it was then." He goes on to say: "When we learnt --" Sorry, excuse me. He goes on to say: "Serbs from Sarajevo retained control over the territory and even extended their territory in some areas, driving the Muslims out of the territories --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're skipping portions, Mr. Jeremy. You're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, when I said "he goes on to say," I meant to alert the witness to my skipping of the portion but I should have made that clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please read the whole of it. So if you would please start: "We even did not know Mr. Karadzic was alive during the first couple of days ..." And then you continue with: "... when we learned that he was alive ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Witness, after the first portion I've read to you,

utterances.speaker: MR. PRSTOJEVIC STATES
utterances.text: "Moreover, we did not know if Mr. Karadzic was alive during the first couple of days. When we learnt that he was alive and when he visited us in Ilidza and encouraged us, the Serbs from Sarajevo retained control over the territory and even extended their territory in some areas, driving the Muslims out of the territories where they had actually been majority." Mr. Guzina, it's correct, isn't it, that you were involved in the driving out of Muslims of territories in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In paragraph 33 of your statement, you state: "In June 1992, I participated in an operation to liberate and capture the residential area around the airport in Dobrinja." This was an operation that involved the removal of non-Serbs from Serb-claimed territories; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June 1992, we set out to liberate either Aerodromsko Naselje because Nedzarici is a Serb neighbourhood and it was under heavy fire from Aerodromsko Naselje. Major Pero Despotovic, who came to Ilidza before that and who took over the Ilidza Brigade, made this decision because the Serbs in Nedzarici could no longer go on that way, the decision was made to take this area so that they could survive. It is true I took part in this operation of taking Aerodromsko Naselje and we did take it. We found very few people there. Where I was, all of these people who were found there were sent to the runway and to the airport building; that is to say, we did not expel anyone or, God forbid, kill anyone. For tactical reasons we simply had to take that neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, when --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war had already started by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: When you refer to "these people," you are referring to Bosnian Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that moment when the decision was made, we did not know how many Muslims were there. We were under fire in Nedzarici and we legitimately set out to liberate that part of the neighbourhood and to stop all this firing at Nedzarici. The war had already started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why don't you answer the question rather than to repeat your own story. The question simply was: When you refer to "these people," whether you were referring to Bosnian Muslims. That was the question. No one said anything about whether it was justified or not. Just who were they you were referring to as "these people." Could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we attacked the Bosnian Muslims. Who else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's who I mean throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then just say "yes." That's the answer to the question. You referred to the Bosnian Muslims. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to move to another document. I wonder if it's a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we do so, I take it that you want to tender this document of -- no, this is already in evidence, I think. It's -- yes. Now, you told us that you sent them to the runway and to the airport building. What happened with them afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They went via Kiseljak onwards to Split. They were all safe and they're all alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did you send them to Kiseljak or did you send them to the runway at the airport building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police were at the airport. And since civilians were obviously not soldiers, we sent them to the police of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza. According to what I know, afterwards they allowed them to go further on via Kiseljak. As far as I know, according to my information, they all remained alive. This is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, that's not what I was asking you. But did -- were they given an option to return to their homes again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not there. I was in the airport neighbourhood. I know that they were sent to the airport, there was a reception centre there. People from the police received them there. And according to what I know, they spent a night there in the camp. And then on the following day, they said where they wanted to go. They were all released. This is what I know and I stand by my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you know that? I mean, my simple -- my question was a very simple one, whether they had an option to return. Now, if I say to someone you can go to A, B, and C, just choose. If that person wants to go to D rather than to A, B, and C, he didn't have that option. So could you please tell me if you know - if you don't know, tell us as well - whether these people were given an option to return to their homes from where they were sent to the runway and to the airport building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, I was not at the airport and I don't know what they were asked. What I'm claiming is that they spent a night --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, whether they spent one night or three nights or seven nights, my question was - and apparently you're unable to answer that - is whether they were given an option to return to their homes because you don't know. Mr. Jeremy, we'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I couldn't be in two places at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming you for anything. I'm just asking you what you do know and what you do not know, and I got an answer. We take a break. If you would follow the usher, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We briefly turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, we left off talking about a June 1992 operation in Dobrinja that you were involved in and I would like to stay on that topic. Now, this was an operation that was carried out in co-ordination with the Main Staff of the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was not an operation at all. It was an action carried out by the Ilidza Brigade. Other units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- all participate in operations as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was clear, whether it's called operation or otherwise, what Mr. Jeremy was talking about. What he wanted to know is whether this action, operation, whatever you call it, whether it was carried out in co-ordination with the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say either yes or no. However, pursuant to an order by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Pero Despotovic the commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't know, tell us. May I remind you of your words in paragraph 33 of your statement: "In June 1992, I participated in an operation ..." And then you describe the operation at the airport. So it is not very appropriate if a question is put to you to comment that. But at the same time I see that in the original it is "akcija" which is mentioned. Apparently "akcija" means "operation," unless there is any challenge to the interpretation. So therefore let's focus on the important things and not on the unimportant ones. You can't give us an answer to the question whether it was in co-ordination with the Main Staff of the VRS. Next question please, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we please see P353. That's the handwritten notebook of Ratko Mladic. I'd like to go to e-court page 166 in the English and 164 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, we see on the page before you that this is an entry in the notebook of Mr. Mladic dated Monday, 15 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to e-court page 170 in the English and 168 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And we see here that there is the numbers 1520, which I take to be a time. The words "conversation with representatives of Sarajevo municipalities." We see number 1, Ilidza, Nedjeljko Prstojevic. Halfway down the page, we see Prstojevic's name underlined and some words underneath which I take to be his comments. The first such comment is that there are 6.500 soldiers in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, no speaking allowed. Even with my earphones on I can hear you. You know what the consequences are. If you want to consult with counsel, you know exactly how to do that. You seem to have forgotten about that little written notes often served you very well. You can consult, but do it at a volume inaudible for us. I can still --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, Mr. Lukic, Mr. Lukic, if Mr. Mladic takes off his earphones he can't hear me anymore. It should be clear that he is not allowed to speak at a volume audible for others. If he wants to consult you, as you may remember, for a long time he was entirely limited to written notes. If it continues as it goes now, we'll return to that system, written notes and no speaking at all. So it's up to Mr. Mladic himself to see whether he wants to go back to that old regime or whether he wants to follow our instructions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, we see the comments of Mr. Prstojevic stating that there are around 6.500 soldiers in Ilidza. Now ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber is fed up with the way in which Mr. Mladic treats this matter. One more loud spoken word and he'll be removed from the courtroom. Let that be clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, referring again to this figure of 6.500 soldiers in Ilidza, you were shown a document today - P3030 - that stated that there were 2.800 individuals in Ilidza in -- who had been -- 2.800 volunteers in Ilidza in March 1992. We then saw a mobilisation order on 6th of April, 1992, P6589. And now in mid-June 1992, we see that there are around six and a half thousand soldiers in Ilidza. Do you recall there being approximately that number of soldiers in Ilidza at this time?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We know that the Ilidza Brigade had approximately 3500 men, the Ilidza Brigade. And the municipality of Ilidza also had part of the Igman Brigade. Perhaps this number has been increased because it also includes some men from the Igman Brigade, because the Igman Brigade covered one part of Hadzici and one part of the territory of the municipality of Ilidza. That's how I explain the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We see towards the bottom of the page there is a subheading: "Requests." And it states, 1: "That officers should plan an operation and take the men to Dobrinja." Now, this is the operation that you were involved in in June 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 171 in the English and 169 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, at the bottom of this page we see the subheading: "Conclusions." Number 1: "To clear the Serbian territory ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please, and focus on the top of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So I've just read on the last page: "To clear the Serbian territory in which Mojmilo and Dobrinja come first." Mr. Guzina, it's correct, isn't it, that this reference to clearing the Serbian territory in which Mojmilo and Dobrinja come first is a reference to the removal of non-Serbs from this area -- these areas?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we go back to the first page that you showed me and then I'll be able to answer your question? If we look at Branko Radan and Danilo Skrba's statements, I can tell you that they were on the other side. They were not physically connected with the municipality of Ilidza. They were on the other side of Dobrinja. We were on one side and they were on the other side, and these are their statements. But these people didn't reside in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, to repeat my question, and if you don't know, then say you don't know. But when we see the subheading: "Conclusions: To clear the Serbian territory in which Mojmilo and Dobrinja come first," that is a reference to the removal of non-Serbs in that area pursuant to the operation that you yourself was involved in; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. I'm not familiar with this document. I've explained why we attacked the airport neighbourhood. The main reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- or the only reason was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't answer the question, we'll just move on and we'll do without what you could tell us about that. You were called by the Defence which means that the Defence considers the information you could provide to us useful, but if you don't answer the questions and tell us all kind of things not asked, then we'll just move on. Mr. Jeremy, next question please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to Exhibit P03059?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, as this document is coming up, I can tell you it's a report from Colonel Tomislav Sipcic of the Romanija Corps to the Main Staff dated 17 June 1992. That's two days after the entry in Mr. Mladic's notebook we just looked at. We see the heading is: "Combat actions in Dobrinja." Paragraph 1, we see a reference to the Ilidza Brigade. Could you read that paragraph 1 and confirm that this refers to the June combat actions in Dobrinja that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Our forces took up the following positions before the night fell: The junction of the Ante Babic and Boro Draskovic Streets, cut off the Rosa Hadzivukovic Street and reach the Ernest Telman Street. They stopped in front of the block of flats in the Marks and Engels Street. Casualties: Three dead and six wounded." Yes, these were the positions we reached in the airport neighbourhood. We took them at that time and that's where we stayed throughout the war. We continued to keep those positions that we took at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to paragraph 6 in this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, if I read the original and this part -- could we go back to the first page. Last line of paragraph 1 is: "Casualties: Three dead and six wounded." Now, in the original, I see the numbers four and six. So I wonder whether there is a risk that the translation is not accurate because if translation of numbers goes already in this direction, then we have to fear even more for text. Please proceed and have it verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we will. Could we refer to paragraph 6 in this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For English it would therefore -- next page, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, we see paragraph 6 states: "The treatment of civilian population: The SRK units are pulling out civilians and taking them to the Lukavica barracks and the prisoners to the Kula KPD. SRBH MUP is classifying civilians according to their ethnicity." Mr. Guzina, this is a reference to the removal of non-Serbs from Serb-claimed territory committed pursuant to the mid-June operation that you were involved in; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't see a reference to the airport neighbourhood here. There was an operation on Dobrinja 1, 2, 3, and 4, all taking place at the same time and we refer to all those as Dobrinja. The forces of the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade attacked from one side and we did from the other. I mentioned prisoners or, rather, civilians who were in the airport neighbourhood and I said that we escorted them to the airport building. Whereas this is the other side, as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Witness, it's your evidence that you escorted civilians, Bosnian Muslim civilians to the airport runway building -- sorry, to the runway or the airport building but not to the Lukavica barracks or the Kula KPD? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my evidence. We escorted them to the airport building, and I'm referring to the people who we found in the airport neighbourhood. There were also Serbs among them. This means that we vacated the neighbourhood of civilians and we escorted them to the airport building. This is what I'm saying and this is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In the same paragraph we see it states: "So Serbs and Croats are being put together and Muslims are being separated from them." You were involved in the separation of Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So the Muslim civilians that you took to the airport facility, the airport runway, and the airport building, somebody else separated them - is that your evidence? - before you escorted them?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not escort them. I was a soldier and I was engaged in taking territory. Soldiers who followed me entered apartments, searched the apartments to see whether there were any civilians there. They gathered them in front of the buildings and then they escorted them to the airport building. All that time I was engaged in taking the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask: Witness, do you mean to say that this whole Dobrinja action or that it was all separate, that it was simultaneously but the whole of Dobrinja was not part of your actions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I'm saying. The Ilidza Brigade launched that action against the airport neighbourhood. That's a fact. On the other side, the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade launched an operation against Dobrinja 1 and 4, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And these --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were two separate actions. We were not co-ordinated in those two actions. We never linked up. Pero Despotovic, who was the brigade commander, I don't know whether he was in co-ordination with the corps. I suppose that he was, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because in paragraph 34 of your statement, I read: "Our plan was to capture the entire area of Dobrinja," which sounds very much as the whole of Dobrinja being the aim of the action.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that it was the whole of Dobrinja, but I am talking about the Ilidza Brigade. Our mission was to take the airport neighbourhood. I don't know what the other units had to do. I suppose that that was their task because that meant life for Ilidza. We were supposed to link up and to join the whole territory of Ilidza; i.e., the part in front of the airport and the part behind it. I suppose that that was the original plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the whole activity was reported in one report, if I understand the document we just looked at well. At least in reporting it was not treated as two entirely separate actions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, as far as I can tell from this report, this report is from the other side, from the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade. There is no reference to the Ilidza Brigade and there is no reference to where our civilians were taken. There is reference to Kula, but that's on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would say the 1st Sarajevo-Romanija Brigade and the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade, both were not at your side -- no, the -- let me see. In paragraph 1, we see the activities of the Ilidza Brigade; paragraph 2, the 1st Sarajevo-Romanija Brigade; and paragraph 3, the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade. Now, what then follows is not -- at least textually not limited to one of the three or two of the three brigades. Nowhere in six I see something like, "The treatment of the civilian population." It says "the SRK units." Now, are all the three brigades mentioned earlier, are they all SRK units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, these are units of the SRK, but I don't see a report from the Ilidza Brigade. If you have that, show it to me and I will confirm that this is indeed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Ilidza Brigade is included in this report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, under 1: Positions taken and how far we got. And this is fine, this is correct. When we took up those positions, we liberated Nedzarici from Muslim forces on the right-hand side. And when we reached those positions in 1992, we remained there and from there we were engaged in decisive defence of Nedzarici. This is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's in your statement. I just put it to you that paragraph 6 is not limited to the other two brigades but makes no distinction whatsoever about the treatment of the civilian population. You have explained and you say, well, that's not true because it doesn't reflect what the Ilidza Brigade did, and I'm inviting you to look at the text and to see where that text supports your recollection. Did you find -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just saying that we did not act unfairly towards people in the airport neighbourhood. We did not ask for their IDs to ascertain whether they were Serbs, Croats, or Muslims. We escorted them to the airport building. And now what happened next, where they were taken, that's another story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not my question. I invited you to see whether the text of paragraph 6 would give any support to your testimony that you didn't take them to Lukavica barracks but that you took them elsewhere. And please carefully listen now to Mr. Jeremy's next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, let's move to a different part of your statement. In paragraphs 33 to 49, you describe your time in the Ilidza Brigade from June 1992 onwards. Now, you were initially appointed commander of the 5th Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade in June 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And towards the end of 1993, with the reorganisation of the Ilidza Brigade, the 5th Battalion became part of the 1st Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade; that's correct, yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When Colonel Radojcic became the commander of the Ilidza Brigade, he reorganised the brigade. He took the 5th, the 3rd, and the 1st Battalions and joined them into one battalion which had about 750 soldiers all together, so it was somewhat bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you were appointed commander of this combined 1st Battalion; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your command of that battalion ceased when the Dayton Agreement was signed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Something goes wrong with the microphone. Could you please restart, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, your command of the 1st Battalion ceased when -- at approximately the time that the Dayton Agreement was signed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, you were wounded on the 23rd of November, 1993, and you spent approximately four months on sick leave; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three to four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you confirmed in the statement that you made in the -- that you provided in the Karadzic case that as a consequence of being wounded, you have no knowledge about a shelling incident that occurred on the 22nd of January, 1994. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please jog my memory, help me to remember? Well, it's possible that that's what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 1D02121, that's Mr. Guzina's statement in the Karadzic case. Could we please go to paragraph 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, the statement on the screen before you is a different statement to the one that you have in your hands. It's the statement you provided in the Karadzic case, and I simply want you to confirm what you say in paragraph 43 in reference to this incident G6. You say the incident was explained to you. It occurred on the 22nd of January, 1994. And skipping some of the text, you go on to say: "I was on sick leave at the time because I had been wounded on the 23rd of November, 1993. I spent about four months on sick leave, and therefore I have no information about this incident."

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my statement. I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'm done with that statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, I'd like to discuss the process of communications in your battalion and communications between your battalion and the Ilidza Brigade command. Now, you discuss this topic during a recorded interview you had with the Office of the Prosecutor in October 2003, and I'm going to put a passage of that interview to you and I'll ask you to confirm it. You were asked: "Q. Did you have a reporting system from the battalion to the brigade?" You answered: "Every day." You were then asked: "Can you explain how that worked? Was it a written report, verbal report, or how was it passed to the brigade?" You answered: "In fact, at the time, every position had induction communication. That's a wire communication system that linked ourselves to our, to the command of the battalion and myself to the brigade command. And I, myself, from the place where I was to the brigade command was just a ten-minute drive by car. Therefore, we were in permanent contact with the brigade and on the communication line. Radojcic introduced that for the reason that it was easy to tap the phones and the, that was a much more secure communication. We knew at any given moment what was going at the positions since the shooting was a daily occurrence. It was not necessary to go to the front lines to learn what was going on." Mr. Guzina, do you stand by the answers that you provided in the recorded interview that I've just quoted back to you?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these are my words, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to a different topic and talk about ammunition used by your battalion and brigade. In paragraph 38 of your statement that you provided in this case, D514, you mention some of the weapons in your battalion. Now, it's correct, isn't it, that the Koran ammunition depot was one of the places where your brigade received its ammunition from?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could the Prosecutor please repeat the name of the depot? I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The name is the Koran, K-o-r-a-n, ammunition depot.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that depot is in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 30790.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question was whether you received your ammunition from that depot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally don't know. We had a commander for logistics who did that job. Where he got the ammunition from, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer to the question was "I don't know," rather than that the Koran depot was in Pale, which -- the location wasn't asked. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, just check the number of the 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. 65 ter 30790, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, before you is a 30 June 1992 SRK request for replenishment of certain ammunition which was sent to the VRS Main Staff and the Koran ammunition depot. Now, I'd like to ask you about a few of the items listed here. The first item requests 7.62-millimetre bullets for PAP semiautomatic rifles, automatic rifles, and PM light machine-guns. It's correct, isn't it, that your brigade had all these types of guns?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And these 7.62 millimetre bullets are the types of bullets that are used with an M-48 rifle, yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: You testified in the Karadzic case that your battalion had M-48 rifles with optic sights. That was at transcript page 31161. Do you stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, could you please check one item. In your question you refer to an M-48 rifle. In the document I see reference to M-84. Could you please check.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did intend to refer to an M-48 rifle notwithstanding the reference of M-84 here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you were referring to item 1 on this list and not to item 2 on this list, if I understood you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, you also testified in the Karadzic case that these M-48 rifles with optical sights were used for sniping. Do you stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never opened any sniper fire there, but I believe this M-72 round is for a heavy machine-gun, M-48. I think that's the case, at least. It needs to be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, I'd like to read you a portion of your testimony in the Karadzic case, and I'll ask you to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, could you give the source to the Defence? The Chamber, of course, doesn't have it available, but I think it's fair that the Defence would be able to verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Transcript page 31161.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: From the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the transcript is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if it's not in evidence, the Chamber usually does not scroll through all the uploaded documents in e-court. So therefore if you want us to have a look at it, please put it on the screen. And that's what we prefer, as a matter of fact, if there's any dispute about what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 30777, e-court page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, I'll read from page 5 -- excuse me, from line 5 on page 31161. "Q. So when we spoke last on Thursday you had just finished telling us that there were no sniper rifles in your battalion and you had no need --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll not see it in your own language. You don't receive --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can hear interpretation, but I don't see it in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, you can't see it in Serbian because there is no Serbian version. It will be read to you and you will receive the translation as the words are spoken by Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Jeremy, could you please restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "Q. So when we spoke last on Thursday, you had just finished telling us that there were no sniper rifles in your battalion and you had no need for sniper rifles because the confrontation line was so close. And you also said that when you were confronted about snipers by UNPROFOR, you of course denied that you had snipers. Do you remember testifying about this? "A. Yes" --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, I'm still reading the quote. "A. Yes. I said that in that part of the Nedzarici I did not have any snipers, but it is a fact that I had M-48 rifles with optic sights. And I think that in the 4th Company of my battalion, there were three snipers that were pointed in the completely opposite direction, Butmir, the airport, not the locations that you mentioned." Mr. Guzina, do you stand by that testimony in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: You went on to state in line 18 -- or you were asked in line 18: "Q. So now I see that you say you had M48 rifles with optic sights, and so were those rifles used for sniping?" And you answered: "Yes." Do you also stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Did you have M48 rifles with optic sights which you used for sniping?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, we had M48 rifles but not for sniping. The Prosecutor said this too quickly so I answered yes, but the answer is we had M48 rifles but not for sniping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they have optic sights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But those are rifles from World War II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, I'll read the next question and the next answer and we'll see if that refreshes your recollection about snipers in your battalion. "Q. You also say that you had -- in the 4th Company of your battalion there were three snipers that were pointed in the completely opposite direction, at the airport, not the locations that you mentioned. I didn't mention any locations. I was talking about snipers generally. So when I asked you last week whether you had snipers, you didn't tell us about these particular snipers, did you?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "A. Obviously we did not understand each other then. The fact is that in terms of these examples of incidents that had occurred, it all has to do with Nedzarici, so I was thinking along those lines; namely, that in Nedzarici there weren't any snipers and there was no mention of targets in Butmir, I mean that is where the snipers were turned and that is why we were thinking at cross-purposes, if you will." Mr. Guzina, again you refer to snipers in your battalion in that answer in the Karadzic case. Is it your position that you were incorrectly interpreted or transcribed and that, in fact, you did not have snipers?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer this question with a yes or no. I have to explain. The fact is we had three snipers in the 4th Company trained at Butmir and the airport runway. I stand by that. We also had M48 rifles with optical sights at certain positions of ours in the 1st Battalion. That, too, is true. However, it is not true that sniper fire was opened and that targets were shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that you had three snipers in your battalion but that the snipers did not open fire at any targets. That's your evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, between M48 rifles from World War II and M75 rifles of the professional JNA, there is a huge difference. M48 rifles are very imprecise weapons from World War II. I really can't answer this with yes or no, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Simply, were the sniper rifles, I'm not talking about the M48 with optic sights but the sniper rifles which you said were in the 4th Company, were they ever used at any target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, against Butmir. Yes, I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us where they were located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the area of Kasindolska Street, facing the airport runway and facing Butmir, the 4th Company of the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, please proceed. It's time for a break, I think. It would be better not to proceed at this moment. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and will resume at 20 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, just to finish our discussion about sniper rifles with a final couple of questions. You testified in the Karadzic case at transcript 31165 that you had at least three M76 sniper rifles in your battalion. My question is: Do you stand by that testimony today?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd like to tender 65 ter 30790 which is the document that we -- that I went through with the witness before we put the transcript on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30790 receives number P6590, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6590 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, I'd like to discuss targeting by your battalion briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do that, anything you are going to deal with 3027? You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, in your Karadzic testimony at transcript page 31185, lines 13 to 14, you stated that: "As the war went on, our targeting got better and better." Do you stand by that testimony today?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And it's correct, isn't it, that after a few weeks of the war you had pre-recorded targets in ABiH-held territory?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As time went on, the number of targets increased because the intelligence we received from Sarajevo helped us expand the target range.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And therefore it helped you to create pre-recorded targets in the ABiH-held territory; correct? I see you --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guzina, you've confirmed that you had approximately 750 men under your command as a battalion commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you will agree that as a commanding officer your actions influenced your subordinates. Yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, you would agree that as a commanding officer your actions influenced your subordinates. Yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I was in command of those people in the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, do you consider the term "poturice" to be a derogatory term for Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Are you aware that individuals who are of Muslim ethnicity may find this term to be offensive?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In February 1993 you were involved in efforts to take Azici; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And Azici is to the north of Ilidza, near Stup; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of the 3rd Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade in the independent detachment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Independent company, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to play you a video in connection with this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 30768a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it need to be played twice, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Stewart informs me the booths have the transcript and it's also been synced in e-court, so we see the words appear on the screen as the clip is played. I'm in your hands as to whether we need to play it twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the issue always is whether -- it's a two-step system. The one is to verify whether the words on the transcript are the same as the words spoken; and then secondly, interpretation of those words. I'm just looking at the booth whether with the information provided, whether we can play it once and that we can be certain that we have an accurate translation. If that is the case, we can play it once; otherwise we would have to play it twice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have never seen this before and we cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's play it twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then play it twice, so that the first round we can verify whether the transcript provided is an accurate one and then in the second round to receive the interpretation. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please play the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Commander, sir, what is the momentary tactical situation in Azici? "Since the attack carried out by poturice, our active defence has become very efficient and we have launched a counterattack. In any case, we are holding this line of defence because it is useful for us. "Another question. Vucko is feeling a bit traumatised because of all the noise so I would like to ask you something on his behalf. When would Vucko get a chance to come back to the centre of town? "Well, I certainly hope it will happen soon. With all soldiers and units at our disposal, it should happen soon. We are waiting for a higher command's order. We would have already been there if they had not prevented us from doing so."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to 24 seconds into that clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So we're now at 25.5 seconds. Mr. Guzina, that is you in the helmet to the left of the screen; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I was younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the person to your left-hand side is Nikola Mijatovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In the video you appear to describe the situation in Azici. Does that pertain to your battalion's activities in that area in February 1993?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was only I from my battalion that took part in this operation. Only along -- because that was the axis that was involved.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the axis be repeated again, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the axis that you referred to, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doglode, that is the village of Doglode, towards the settlement of Azici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So, Witness, to confirm when you refer to activities in Azici, you are referring to your own activities in Azici in February 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the activities of the Ilidza Brigade. Of course, I used some of these words in my own name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And these are the actions that you were involved in yourself in February 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.
