utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to 44 seconds in that clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, is this the area of Azici that we see as viewed from your positions?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know from where this picture was taken, I mean, from this film. But this is Azici. Specifically this detail, I don't know exactly where this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Well, my last question on this clip is: It was you that used the term "poturice" while speaking in front of your men. Yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender that clip as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30768a receives number P6591, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, staying on this Azici operation, I would like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we please see 65 ter 30769.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this is an excerpt from the final report of the United Nations Commission of Experts. So the document on the screen before you concerns the Azici operation, and this is a page that is included in this May 1994 report to the Secretary-General regarding events in Sarajevo. It specifically refers to the Azici operation and it includes an interview with you with Reuters dated 24 February 1993. Let's look at paragraph 1635, which states: "Narrative of Events: "Serb forces were reported to have captured the key western suburb of Azici. A Reuters television crew went into the suburbs on Tuesday and found it 'completely destroyed.' Heavy fighting broke out nearly two weeks ago when the Serbs attacked the western suburbs." And skipping some of the text, it goes on to state: "The Serbs" -- Halfway into that paragraph: "The Serbs attacks on Azici and Stup followed a BiH government push against the Serb-held stronghold of Ilidza. On some days, more than a thousand shells were reported to have fallen in the contested areas. The Serbs said that they had captured Azici without a single soldier killed and only a handful wounded. 'We don't want to lose more soldiers, so we decided on a new tactic: We destroy a place before we occupy it,' said Svetozar Guzina, deputy commander of the Serb forces in the area." Mr. Guzina, that's your quote provided to Reuters; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So it's correct that in February 1993, notwithstanding your ability to target accurately, which we discussed earlier, here you decided to destroy the entire place; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that we attacked Azici because we were under fire from there all the time. It is correct that we attacked Azici to rectify our own lines so that the line of the 3rd Battalion would be more efficient. It is correct that we used a lot more shells because our assessment was that the Muslim forces in that area were very strong, exceptionally strong. And it is also true that civilians were not living there and we used as much weaponry as we needed to take Azici. That is correct. You see for yourself that the operation was efficient. We only had a few wounded men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, again, why not answer the question? I mean, you tell us what is correct but that was not what Mr. Jeremy asked you about. You could have told us what the weather was, you could have told us anything. The question was a different one. The question was that notwithstanding your ability to target accurately, that you decided to destroy the entire place. Whether that is correct, that was the question, and would you please answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's very hard to answer just with a yes or no. There were 10 or 15 houses there in that settlement and also a factory where socks were being manufactured. That is what we were supposed the take in order to rectify the line. That is what is correct. I cannot just answer with a yes or no. Yes, we used that much ammunition. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Guzina, I'm not asking you to answer by yes or no, but I'm asking you to answer with a focus on the question. Now, in the second round you at least made an attempt. You said there were 15 houses and a factory. Did you decide that those had to be destroyed despite of your ability to accurately target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because in all of those houses and in that factory there were positions of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, it's your evidence, is it not, that you took steps to ensure that there were no civilians living in Azici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In response to my earlier question, you stated that: "It is also true that civilians were not living there," and by "there" you're referring to Azici. So my question is: On what basis was it true that there were no civilians in Azici before you targeted the entire area?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the intelligence that was received at the brigade claimed that there were no civilians in that area. That was sufficient for us to do what we did. And I think, I think to this day, 20-odd years later, that this is an operation that was successfully carried out. Even after this case, no one said anything about civilian casualties, UNPROFOR, no one else. At least I have never received such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender that document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30769 receives number P6592, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. The reason why I was a bit hesitant to immediately continue, Mr. Jeremy, is about paragraph 6036 on our screen. And the Hadziska [phoen] mosque, is that in the area where this action was taken or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not my area. That's the area of the Igman Brigade. It's at a completely different part of the front line, Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, staying on the topic of civilian casualties, I'd like to refer you to a question and answer provided in -- during your testimony in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 30777. That's the witness's testimony in the Karadzic case. In particular, e-court page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, I'm going to read to you a question put to you by Mr. Karadzic and I'll read you your answer and ask you to --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have English, both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I told you before that this is transcript of your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and you'll hear the translation when Mr. Jeremy reads portions of it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Guzina. I'll read the excerpt now. "Q. I'd just like to put a few questions to you. In your statement here, you said that you never issued an order to fire at civilians, and that your subordinates never issued such orders. Nevertheless, did it happen that civilians would get killed on both sides? "A. Yes. "Q. How would that happen? How do you explain that if it was not on orders? "A. At any rate, it wasn't on orders. It is a fact that there were civilian casualties on both sides. However, I can say freely that this is collateral damage on both sides. Civilians who happened to be on the front line. No one wanted to kill them. They simply happened to be there because fire that had been opened was not individual fire. It was automatic gun-fire. There was a lot of bullet dispersion on both sides and therefore civilian casualties could not be avoided. "As far as the Serb side is concerned, at least in my commanding the 1st Battalion, civilians were ordered not to go to their homes. It was forbidden. But simply people went to their homes to see their houses, to see their property, to see whether everything was in proper order, and that is how quite a few ended up getting killed." Mr. Guzina, do you stand by your testimony in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to the subject of sniping with you. Now it's correct, isn't it, that your battalion had positions in the faculty of theology and the school for the blind in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the battalion, my battalion, the 1st Battalion had positions at the faculty of theology and the school for the blind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you marked those positions in -- on a map during your testimony in the Karadzic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 30787. That's the marked map I just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, do you -- could you please confirm on the screen before you that the T marked in red indicates the faculty of theology? Could you please confirm that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could you confirm that the B indicates the school for the blind?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there any disagreement about these being the locations? And isn't it true that they were marked already also on the previous map which was then remarked by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that there is no dispute. But just a moment, please. May I take a look? I think that in one of the documents that we tendered this had been marked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is properly marked, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D02125. It has a new D number and it also has a marking for the school for blind children, so there is no dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the only dispute could be that the school for the blind is now the school for the blind children, and I think that is what it is, Mr. Jeremy, isn't it? So you have added slightly to the confusion. And D517 gives us just as much information as this newly marked map, isn't it? And on matters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And in addition, we have D519 as marked by the witness in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, and it doesn't add anything to the evidence we have received already in this respect. You insist on tendering it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In which case, Your Honours, if it's clear to you, then I don't insist on tendering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, you yourself have been to the school for the blind many times; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: School for the blind children you refer to, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The school for the blind children, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The correct wording is "Zavod za slepu decu," that is to say, Institute for Blind Children. So I believe that we have already dealt with that previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we know exactly where we are and how it is called. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see Exhibit Number P01065.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, as this is being brought to our screens, I'll tell you it's a daily situation report from UNMO dated 11 July 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page -- or I note the date is 11 January 1994. Could we please go to page 4 -- sorry, it's page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We see number 2: "Warring Party Activity." And under d, we see: "UNMOs confirm from the spot as well as hospital visit 1 X Bosnian CIV male" --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm on number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We should be in -- could we have a look at the previous page or is it -- Mr. Jeremy, we are looking at the warring party activity, where is that to be found? Or the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honours, and I'll look for the B/C/S equivalent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently there is something ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we go to page 6 in the B/C/S, please. Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So referring to part d of number 2, we see it states: "UNMOs confirm from the spot as well as hospital visit 1 X Bosnian civilian male (age 17) injured by sniping at BP863578 near the house for blind people at Alipasino Polje area at," and then there is a code. "It is suspected that the sniping came from," another code, "BSA side. It may be highlighted that this is the third casualty (all civilians) in the same spot in the last few days." Mr. Guzina, I'd also like to show you another document a day later and then I'll ask you some questions on both of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P1079.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, this is an UNMO daily situation report dated 13th of July -- sorry, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: It's now gone from my screen. I don't know if others have it on their screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It went to power-saving mode temporarily. There we are again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, this is an UNMO report dated the 12th of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it 12th or 13th, Mr. Jeremy?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: 13th of July, Your Honour. Thank you for that clarification. It's the sitrep for the 12th but dated the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, in paragraph 24 of this document we read as follows, heading: "Other important incidents/patrols/investigation: "a. UNMOs were allowed by the 4th BiH Brigade to patrol along CFL," and some locations are referred to for the first time. b, which I'm interested in, states: "Command 1st Battalion of BSA Ilidza Brigade admitted the sniping by BSA from BP 859578 (house for blind people). He promised that there would be no more sniping from that place." Mr. Guzina, it was you as commander of the 1st Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade at the time of these reported sniping incidents that admitted to the sniping from the house for the blind people; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was the commander of the 1st Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade. And no, I didn't admit that, and I don't stand by the statement that sniper fire came from that building. This is just either a randomly written sentence or mistranslated. I don't know who did it. It's not correct that I admitted that because we simply didn't do it. It is possible that I said that I would check whether by chance somebody opened fire from those positions, but to admit that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Do you recall checking whether there had been sniping from that place on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after this conversation and in the Karadzic case we discussed the same case. However, after the conversation with the French captain who came to the scene because he was a UN observer, I checked. My soldiers told me that they didn't open fire and I believed them. The fact is that in the entire area there was no need for sniper fire. If they told me that somebody had been hit with a burst of fire, I would have believed them. Not with a sniper. My decisive defence in my battalion was cross-fire and every soldier had to be able to open a salvo, not individual bullets. That was my standing order throughout the four years of war. If you know that the 104th, 122nd, and the Butmir Battalion were facing my lines throughout the war, you can understand how we felt in my battalion all that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Do you recall passing on this complaint that you received from UNPROFOR to your brigade command?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in all of those matters we briefed our brigade commander. I believe that the brigade commander was in the picture because it was my duty to convey to him how Muslims used UNPROFOR to accuse us of things without any proof. I believe that I informed the brigade commander of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do you recall what response you got from your brigade commander on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, it was to pay attention to the lines, that it was not in our best interest to provoke them. The fact was that we allowed UNPROFOR to come to our front lines to control the situation and to check the accusations of the Muslim forces who were telling them that we were constantly opening fire. That's why UNPROFOR was on our side on the tallest building. We allowed UNPROFOR to position themselves there instead of us, because they had to control the line between the two warring parties in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So to clarify, in this particular case you do not recall what response you got from your brigade commander; yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that sense he supported me. He told me not to do such things and we didn't. I can't really quote him. I can't remember word for word parts of that meeting. If you have any minutes, you can show them to me. But I know that from our superior command, we always received orders not to open fire on civilians because it was not in the interest of the Serbian army because we had already won the war at that moment and we were only waiting for political means to put a seal on that situation. Obviously, the Muslim forces kept on provoking us in order to incite UNPROFOR and to convey a message to the international community that we Serbs were to be blamed for everything. But in this particular case, this was certainly not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, I put it to you that the two documents, the two UN documents we have just seen show that civilians were killed from sniper fire originating from the house for the blind children. Do you accept that that was the case?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not saying that they didn't get killed. I suppose that they did. But I claim with full responsibility that it was not due to sniper fire. If I'd been told that an individual bullet hit a child or an elderly woman, I would have said that it was possible because our rifles were set on salvo fire. But I claim with full responsibility that we didn't open sniper fire from those positions because it was against our interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, it's correct, isn't it, that no disciplinary steps were ever taken against any soldiers in your battalion in response to accusations of sniping Bosnian Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. No measures were taken because we did not open fire on civilians. And this is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to scheduled sniping incident F9 which you discussed in paragraph 47 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, I've read the statement in that respect. Could we first inquire whether the witness has any knowledge about the incident itself rather than drawing conclusions from what he may have heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, it's actually correct, isn't it, that you have no personal knowledge of sniping incident F9?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I heard of that was in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss a document, an SRK combat report, that you refer to in the same paragraph 47 of your statement and that you connect to this particular sniping incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see 1D02122.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, this is Exhibit D518, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see Exhibit D518, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, during the Karadzic case, you were asked if you were aware that the sniping incident that you've just commented on occurred at 7.00 or 7.30 in the evening on the 26th of June, and you confirmed that you were not aware of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this has been recorded, then that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now this document on the screen before us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, is there any disagreement that the recorded words are as they were presented by Mr. Jeremy? Because otherwise we end up with an assumption which is not verified, that those were the words of this witness. Any dispute about what the witness said in Karadzic in this respect, Mr. Stojanovic? No, no dispute about that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, this document dated 26th of June, 1994, and timed at 1700 hours refers to a series of events that occurred at particular times and at particular locations. Let's start with the times. So the first times referenced are 2020 hours and 2215 on the 25th of June, 1994, so the day before this particular sniping incident. And again I see and I make the point that this combat report is timed at 1700 hours on the 26th of June. So, Mr. Guzina, it's correct, isn't it, that all the events referred to in this document are the night before or at the very least two hours before the sniping incident that was described to you; yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says that all that activity took place on the 25th of June, 1994. In the next paragraph it says, and I apologise, engineering works were taking place in the Sucura Kuca [phoen] sector, which is in Nedzarici. I suppose that we opened fire to make things stop, although this is not mentioned in here. It says here that we complained to the UN, they came, and they put a stop to those works immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, let's take a look at the locations referred to in this first paragraph, and these are the locations from where firing is suggested to have originated from on to Serb positions. So first, Kovaci and Glavogodina. Now, they are in the Hrasnica area, correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sector of the 2nd Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade. That's before you reach Hrasnica from Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the Vrutci, V-r-u-t-c-i, sector, that's at the west end of Ilidza at the foot of Mount Igman; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, in the area of defence of the 2nd Battalion. And yes, it is at the foot of Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Fire is also indicated to have come from the direction of the cold storage plant. That's in Stup, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, when exactly was the incident reported to have taken place? 26th of June, 7.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why are we then going into any detail? When the witness says that this document dated the 26th of June which reports the situation at 5.00 p.m., then I don't need to go through the whole of that document to find out that what is found in this document cannot -- well, if there is any claim to this explaining what happened at 7.00, then I would say let's look at the report of the next day to see. But to go into all the details of this, is there really a need for that? Witness, would you agree that the report which was describing the situation finishing two hours before the incident could not possibly explain what happened at two hours after that moment where the report was said to -- to describe the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Judge, sir. And I will give the same answer for the previous questions. The positions were the same. I already answered that question. It was a Muslim provocation, nothing else. And the same goes for the Institute for the Blind and the sniping from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's all Muslim provocations and thus -- but you said on the basis of this document that this alleged incident - alleged meaning that it was not true, I do understand - can be attributed to what is written down in this report. Would you agree with me if the report describes the situation at 5.00 p.m., that it cannot reasonably explain what happened at 7.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this makes sense, that you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That concludes my examination on this particular area, Your Honours. I know we're at break time. I've got one more area to move to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll first take a break. Could the witness follow the usher. We take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, just one observation. Earlier as well you compared the statement of this witness with his Karadzic statement. Now, an area was left out, I think it was G8, and in that statement I think that he had said that he doesn't know anything about it. Why to revisit here where apparently, perhaps logically, it's taken out of the statement, to deny something which doesn't even appear in his statement? Or at least to seek confirmation of something which is apparently, and most likely on purpose, is left out? Perhaps you find it during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll respond to that after the break, if that's all right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to follow-up on your question about incident G6. My intention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was G6, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: My intention by drawing attention to that was simply given the importance of this scheduled incident, I simply wanted to draw the Chamber's attention to the fact that the witness had no personal knowledge of this incident, that he was on sick leave at this time. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's not in the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but he had not given any statement about G6, so therefore to say he doesn't know about something he doesn't talk about, I would expect most witnesses not to know anything about matters which they are not giving statements about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: My thinking, Your Honours, was simply to exclude the possibility that any general comments could pertain on that incident, but I certainly take the point you've made to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, you had regular contact with the French UNPROFOR troops situated at the airport; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the orders of the corps and the brigade commander, I had daily contact with UNPROFOR and their liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Do you recall setting up a meeting in your capacity as -- or do you recall setting up a meeting through UNPROFOR liaison officers in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you explain to me what this is about, I might remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we please see Exhibit P751. And the original is written in French, but if we could just please have on our screens the English and the B/C/S translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, this is a 9 July 1995 UNPROFOR memorandum from a Captain Guegan to Colonel Meille, deputy commander of Sector Sarajevo. The subject of the memorandum is a meeting between Captain Guegan and a liaison officer of the Ilidza Brigade, Captain Novak Prodanovic. Now, Captain Prodanovic was your brigade's liaison officer; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Novak Prodanovic was a liaison officer first in my battalion and then he moved to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: According to the second paragraph this meeting was instigated by a first contact on 8 July with Captain Svetozar Guzina, aka, Sesa. Captain Guegan contacted you to arrange this meeting, yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The paragraph goes on to say: "It seems that the meeting has been approved by General Milosevic, commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps by phone conversation heard by S/O interpreter of BATINF 2." Do you recall obtaining General Milosevic's approval for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was obviously a mistake there and there's a mistake here when it says that the commander of the 1st Battalion was based in Nedzarici. I was based in Kasindolska Street. The second mistake is that I couldn't skip Colonel Radojcic and speak to General Milosevic, the brigade commander, so I believe the interpreter must have misheard and this is misquoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you there. The question was not to find all the mistakes in the report, but the question was whether you recall that General Milosevic had approved the meeting. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, in the next paragraph we read that: "The liaison officer arrived at the 1st Battalion CP at 0900 hours today." Were you present at this meeting? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have been. I probably was. You have to know that every single day I had contacts with the UNPROFOR. And if it is written here, it's probably true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 3 in this document, please, in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, during this meeting, Captain Novak Prodanovic points out a number of facts to the UNPROFOR liaison officer. Now, directing your attention to the middle of the page of the B/C/S translation, which is the last page of the English version, one of the facts acknowledged by Captain Prodanovic was "that Krema rockets had been fired on the city of Sarajevo (about a dozen)." Mr. Guzina, is it correct that Krema rockets were -- was the expression that you used to refer to rockets that had been modified with aerial bombs?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this name, Krema. Never heard it before. I knew about modified rockets that had been fired, but I never heard this name before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The next sentence in this paragraph indicates that Captain Prodanovic further explained: "This was psychological warfare aimed at upsetting the Bosnian soldiers engaged on the Treskavica front who would be worried about the safety of their families in Sarajevo." Mr. Guzina, is it correct that the SRK fired on the city of Sarajevo when combat operations were taking place elsewhere outside of the city, like the Treskavica front, for example?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, we used these rockets but only on legitimate targets in Sarajevo and for the special units of the army and the police, when Muslim civilians were allowed to leave Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In the next few sentences --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, Witness, why not answer the question? The question was whether the SRK fired on the city in response to or at least in relation to combat operations which were taking place elsewhere in the country. That was the question. Not whether you fired at legitimate targets. Not -- listen to the question and please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've heard about this activity but I was never on site when these rockets were fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the question again is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it was not in my area of responsibility. You should ask the brigade commander if he ever comes here. It was his job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no knowledge about rockets being fired in relation to events that happened somewhere else in the country, but the rockets nevertheless being fired at Sarajevo? You have no knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard about it but I didn't see it with my own eyes. That's the kind of knowledge I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, you can't see with your own eyes that it is in relation to combat operations elsewhere in the country, because that's -- you only can learn about that. Are you aware of any firing of projectiles on the city of Sarajevo which was in direct relation to events which happened outside the Sarajevo theatre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously we didn't understand each other. What I am saying is this: The firing of air rockets at the city of Sarajevo was not done from my area of responsibility. Second, I was not present when these rockets were fired from the area of the Ilidza Brigade. Third, the fact is we had orders during Muslim offensive at Treskavica and elsewhere outside our area of responsibility, we had orders from our staff to locate one target in the area of our battalion and try to capture it in order to distract Muslim forces from leaving Sarajevo, to bring them back by making them believe that we would continue to fire at the city and such things happened. I know about that. There was one feature like that that we chose on the orders of the Main Staff at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of the hill.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is the case that I mentioned in -- that was mentioned in the report that was shown to me during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you said "on the orders of the Main Staff at" and then you referred to a hill. Could you repeat what hill you referred to there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned Betonara, a concrete building located on the first combat line, a building where the Muslims were. I don't remember mentioning a hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, in the next few sentences we read the following: "In fact, two Krema rockets were launched on the Television building. One of them hit it and consequently, according to Captain Novak, journalists might have reported on the incident and the Bosnian soldiers were informed about the existence of these weapons called Terror." Mr. Guzina, it's correct, isn't it, that the Ilidza Brigade fired these modified rockets hoping that they would hit the inside of the city of Sarajevo and be reported as weapons of terror; yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's true. But to me, the television building was a legitimate target. At the very beginning I went into that building before the war even began, and I saw inside a lot of weapons. The television building was a legitimate target to me, especially since they spread propaganda long before the war. As for the rest, you could call that captain and ask him. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Witness, you've just mentioned the television building. The captain acknowledged that Krema rockets were fired on the city of Sarajevo and he referred to about a dozen. Is it your position that the city of Sarajevo was a -- also a legitimate target?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I said the television building was a legitimate target. I didn't say the other thing. You are trying to put words into my mouth. It's true I have been here for four hours, but I'm still able follow what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Guzina, you would agree that the use -- that these modified aerial bombs were used on the city of Sarajevo as a means of psychological warfare; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you. You should ask that question of the brigade commander and the corps commander, the people who issued those orders. In my area of responsibility it didn't happen. I could only give you my opinion, but it's not qualified, concerning these rockets. I am not a expert for aerial bombs, how much damage they can cause, and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guzina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Stojanovic, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm also looking at the clock. If you would be able to conclude today, that, of course, would be preferable. At the same time, I don't want to put any pressure upon your re-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court P3059 again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have already answered questions on this document. I would like to ask you to concentrate on point 6, where we read: "The treatment of civilian population: "SRK units are pulling civilians out and into the Lukavica barracks, whereas prisoners are put into" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: -- "KP Dom Kula --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have the second page in English on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it -- is the Lukavica barracks outside your area?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer. Is it or is it not outside your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was outside my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is the Lukavica barracks outside of the area of responsibility of the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's also outside the area of the Ilidza Brigade. We have no connection with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the KPD Kula. Is this building outside the area of defence of your battalion and your brigade?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's on the other side of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the purpose of extracting civilians to the Lukavica barracks clear to you and what was it?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we extracted civilians to the airport building, these commanders also extracted their civilians to those buildings to save their lives and later exchange them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the intensity of the fighting such that there could have been collateral damage among civilians?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we hadn't done that, many civilians would have been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One short question between. You said civilians, to save their lives and to later exchange them. Were civilians subject to exchange or were they free to go wherever they wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were able to go wherever they wanted, but the people who captured them would see their IDs, would see who they were, and decide whether they were free to go wherever they wanted because there were soldiers among these civilians. I think that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- okay on our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the whole reference to exchange is a slip of the tongue or is not true? Because exchanges, if you change -- exchange one person for another, you give me that person, I give you this person, so that did not -- that was just a mistake that you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question. I said if there were any soldiers among them, they would be exchanged. The other civilians had freedom of movement. That's what I wanted to emphasize.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you are recorded to have said: "These commanders also extracted their civilians to those buildings to save their lives and later exchange them." Is it your claim that you said at that time that to save their lives and if there were found soldiers among them, then that these soldiers would then be exchanged? Is it your claim that you said that? Or did you say to save their lives and later exchange them referring to civilians in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember well, I said all civilians that we found in the airport neighbourhood without any distinction, we didn't see their IDs right there, we evacuated them straight to the airport building where the civilian police was in charge of checking their IDs. And if there were any soldiers among them, according to our intelligence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may have used that in the second round, although not in the same words, as an explanation, but your first statement was about saving the life of civilians and then exchange them. Do you contest that that's what you said? Because then we'll verify it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible that I said that, but my thinking is what I'm telling you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was asking you about what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I try to clear something here with you, Mr. Witness. I think what Mr. Stojanovic is talking to you about are the civilians that were taken to Kula KPD and the Lukavica barracks which you say were outside your area of responsibility. He's not talking about the people that you sent to the airport, as I understand him. And these are the people who were outside the area which you say where the civilians were exchanged, so don't confuse that question with the people that came to the airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now listen carefully to the next question that Mr. Stojanovic will put to you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I understand of the question by the lawyer, it was the same operation. Only the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade and the Ilidza Brigade were attacking Dobrinja and they extracted civilians to different places on their respective sides. That's how I understood the question. Because I don't even know what's -- what was happening in Kula. It was my assumption that that's what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The last question on this document. In this activity, at any point in time, did you have orders to evacuate the civilian population from Dobrinja against their will?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't have such orders. I claim that with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point you were asked whether the term "poturice" that you had occasion to hear was considered by you as derogatory. You said no. Could you please tell the Court why you did not use that term in a negative context?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because "poturice," in my mind, is a convert and people converted to a different faith during the Ottoman empire. And we know from history that many Muslim names were new names taken by formerly Serb-named families and I don't think that's an offence to the Muslims. Just as we call them the Bosniaks today, before that we called them Muslims, and even before that we called them "poturice," meaning Turkish converts. I don't know if this explanation is good enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to finish with a question related to the document of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the 26th of July at 1700 hours, that was before the break. The combat activities precisely along that line of the defence sector of your battalion, were they of such intensity that that could be treated by way of every day fighting?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can guarantee and claim with full responsibility that the area of my battalion, the 1st Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade, was the worst line in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps for the following reasons: We had a very unfavourable situation, an enormous number of high-rise buildings in Dobrinja that are not in this map at all, Mojmilo hill which is dominant in that area. Then Sokolje which is dominant in that area. Whoever was in that area knows the situation under which we waged war. Many soldiers from the Ilijas, Vogosca, Rajlovac Brigade, not to mention the Ilidza Brigade, they came to Nedzarici by way of punishment. They were penalised. There could have been no greater punishment than being there and being in Aerodromsko Naselje.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not hear Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, first of all you referred to the 26th of July. May I take it that that was a slip of the tongue, that you refer to the 26th of June. Yes, and you announced this as, I think, your last question. So we know that there are usually ten more to follow, but could you perhaps really put your last question then to the witness. Well, or not more than two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I will finish with this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This fighting in the area of the Institute for Blind Children, in view of this last answer of yours, could that be treated as daily fighting, daily combat?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the institute, Vitkovici, the red house, the airport neighbourhood, every day there was fighting. And what I stated a moment ago, I think that you heard that, my order was that there should be bursts of gun-fire using automatic weapons simply because the line was so close and it was possible for the Muslims to enter our positions by running over these 30 or 40 metres. That could have happened at any moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for having testified today.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR GUZINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for having asked me to come. I hope that I was of use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, any further questions triggered by the re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Guzina, since the Chamber has no further questions for you either, this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, which is quite a journey, and to have answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, for tomorrow, the Chamber was informed that the - and I think we can deal with it in open session - the medical examination could be postponed until 3.00. The Chamber also inquired into the time needed for lunch and the Chamber received information that Mr. Mladic usually gets his lunch package with him and that there is no need to reserve extra time for that. So therefore it seems that the presence of Mr. Mladic tomorrow can be secured and we don't have to give up on this one session. Mr. Weber, you're about to be on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. This afternoon there is a matter that came to the Prosecution's attention in conjunction with the proofing note for the next witness, and it's actually an urgent matter that relates to the next witness that's to be heard tomorrow. Ms. Hasan is present and is available to address the matter briefly with the Chamber before we break today, if that's possible. If not, we could further address it through other means, but it does relate to the next testimony -- the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course it comes as a surprise to us as well. I'm trying to finish on time and then -- is Ms. Hasan in a position to explain it in one minute or one minute and a half, so that we know at least what we are talking about and that we also know whether we have to further discuss it in court or whether it can be dealt with in a different way this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Just to try and encapsulate the issue here. The next witness, Mr. Milorad Batinic, had a statement filed with a 92 ter package, and a few days after the filing of that statement we received a witness acknowledgement with a signature. In receiving the proofing note, which arrived yesterday evening, it occurred to me that the paragraph numbering referenced there for corrections and additions to the statement did not match the original statement filed to the 92 ter package. Going on to e-court, I discovered that the -- a new statement, if I can call it that, has been uploaded. The statement that has been uploaded comprises of five pages in B/C/S, six in English, whereas the old statement, the original one, was nine pages in English. With changes to the statement, additions, I haven't gone through it in detail, done a comparison, and the signature appended to the, what I'm calling the new statement, is -- bears the same date as the witness acknowledgement appended to the original statement. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- I'm quite perplexed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps at this moment we ask for a brief explanation in one minute. Has it got anything to do with copying and pasting statements from previous cases because that -- I would not -- Mr. Lukic, any explanation for this mysterious two versions signed on the same date?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have only one in front of me. I will have to check with my Case Manager and I will contact Ms. Hasan as soon as I check [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then we will hear whether the matter will be resolved. Otherwise, we'll hear tomorrow morning where we stand and whether the Prosecution is in a position to cross-examine the witness and what statement will be tendered. We do not know yet, but it's -- what you told us certainly would require thorough attention, Mr. Lukic, not only on what the situation is but also how that situation arose. We leave it to that at this moment. And with our thanks to all those assisting us for four minutes longer than expected, we adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 12th of June, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 12th day of June, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.20 p.m.,
